title: Abimelech, the Bramble King
summary: Abimelech, Gideon's son by a concubine from Shechem, persuades his mother's kin to back him, hires thugs with money from Baal's temple, and murders his seventy half-brothers on one stone; only Jotham escapes. Crowned king at Shechem, Abimelech is denounced by Jotham in a fable of trees who make a thornbush their king. After three years God sends ill will between Abimelech and Shechem, and the two destroy each other: Abimelech razes Shechem and burns its tower, then dies at Thebez when a woman drops a millstone on his head, and Jotham's curse is fulfilled.
story: Chapter 8 ended with Gideon refusing a crown, naming his son Abimelech (my father is king), and Israel turning to Baal-berith. Chapter 9 shows where that leads. It is the only chapter in the book's central section without a foreign oppressor, without a cry to the LORD, and without a deliverer. The enemy is inside Israel, and the violence is between brothers and neighbors. It is the book's first experiment with kingship, and it is a disaster, a warning that stands behind every later discussion of kings in Israel. The chapter also shows the downward spiral of chapter 2 at work: the son of a judge becomes the oppressor.
historical:
Shechem, between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim, was a major Canaanite city with a long history before Israel, and it seems to have kept a mixed population, loyal to Baal-berith (or El-berith, God of the covenant). Gaal's appeal to the men of Hamor, the father of Shechem (verse 28), recalls the Canaanite ruling family of Genesis 34 and suggests local, non-Israelite loyalties. Excavations at Tell Balata, ancient Shechem, uncovered a massive fortress-temple of the Middle and Late Bronze Ages. The excavator G. Ernest Wright and others connected it with the temple of El-berith and the tower of Shechem in this chapter, though that identification is debated.

Beth-millo probably means house of the fill, perhaps a fortified platform or citadel district. Thebez is usually identified with Tubas, northeast of Shechem, though this is not certain. Abimelech's death was remembered in Israel as a proverbial example: centuries later, Joab expected King David to ask, who struck down Abimelech? Was it not a woman with a millstone? (2 Samuel 11:21).
cultural:
Abimelech's appeal to his mother's brothers used kinship: in the ancient world, family and clan were the basic political loyalties, and a son of a Shechemite concubine could claim to be their own flesh and blood. Money from a temple treasury funded his campaign, showing how tightly religion and politics were bound together. Murdering rival heirs was a common way for ancient rulers to secure power; the killing of all seventy on one stone suggests a public execution.

Fables in which plants or animals speak were known in the ancient Near East, and Jotham's is one of the few in the Bible (compare 2 Kings 14:9). The olive, fig, and vine were the most valued plants of the land, producing oil, fruit, and wine. The thornbush (buckthorn or bramble) offered no real shade and was dangerous in dry seasons because it easily caught fire, which could spread to the forests. Sowing a city with salt (verse 45) was a symbolic curse, marking a place as barren and uninhabitable. The upper millstone was a hand-held stone that women used daily to grind grain on a lower stone; it was heavy enough to kill. To die at a woman's hand was considered shameful for a warrior, so Abimelech had his armor-bearer finish him.
literary: The chapter is built on retribution. Jotham's fable (verses 7 to 21) sits at its center and interprets everything around it. His conditional curse, that fire may come from Abimelech and consume Shechem and fire from Shechem consume Abimelech, is fulfilled in the rest of the chapter, which the narrator underlines in verses 56 and 57: God repaid Abimelech and brought the wickedness of Shechem back on their heads. There are careful echoes. Seventy brothers are killed on one stone; Abimelech is killed by one stone. Abimelech burns the tower of Shechem; he dies trying to burn the tower of Thebez. The episode with Gaal and Zebul (26 to 41) is almost comic, with Gaal's boasts and Zebul's mocking reply that he sees the shadows of the mountains. The narrator avoids calling Abimelech a judge; he is a king who reigned over Israel (verse 22), a different kind of ruler.

outline.t: Abimelech murders his brothers and is made king
Jotham's fable of the trees and his curse
God sends ill will between Abimelech and Shechem
Abimelech destroys Shechem and burns its tower
Abimelech's death at Thebez and the curse fulfilled

doctrines.note: The narrator states outright that God repaid the wickedness of Abimelech and of Shechem (verses 56 and 57). Evil turns back on those who commit it, and God oversees that return, even when he works through the violence of the guilty themselves.
Jotham's fable mocks the idea that a worthless man can offer real protection. The chapter warns that kingship grasped by violence and without God brings destruction rather than shelter.

God is not named as acting in the first part of the chapter, but he sends the ill will that begins the end (verse 23). He works through human choices, grievances, and even a woman's desperate act to bring justice.

words.note: Atad, thornbush or bramble. In Jotham's fable it is the only plant willing to reign, and it offers shade it cannot give and fire it can. The image fits Abimelech: worthless as a protector, dangerous as a destroyer.

Malakh, to reign as king. It runs through the fable, as the trees ask each plant to reign over them. Israel's first attempt at kingship comes not from God's choice but from a man's ambition, and the verb carries that irony.

Ba'al, lord, master, or owner. The leaders of Shechem are literally the ba'als (lords) of Shechem, the same word as the name of the god. The wordplay links the city's rulers with the god whose temple funded Abimelech.

Shuv, to return, here meaning to repay or bring back. God returned Abimelech's evil to him and brought Shechem's evil back on their own heads (verses 56 and 57). The verb names the principle of the chapter: evil comes home.

christ: Abimelech is a picture of the kind of king Israel did not need: one who seizes power by murder, offers a shade he cannot give, and destroys his own people. Jotham's fable asks who is fit to reign, and it leaves the question open. The New Testament presents Jesus as the king who did the opposite, who came not to be served but to serve and to give his life (Mark 10:45), and under whose shade his people truly find refuge. The olive, the fig, and the vine, the plants that refused to rule, are also images used for Israel and for Christ's people (Romans 11, John 15). The connection is thematic: the chapter shows the need for a true king by showing a false one.

hard.q: What does it mean that God sent a spirit of animosity between Abimelech and Shechem?
hard.a: Verse 23 says God sent a spirit, literally an evil or harmful spirit, that led to the breakdown. Similar language appears when a harmful spirit from God troubles Saul (1 Samuel 16:14). Some interpreters understand it as a personal spiritual being permitted or sent by God as an agent of judgment. Others read it as a way of describing a mood of hostility and distrust that God allowed to arise between two guilty parties. Across these views, the text's point is that God is sovereign over the working out of judgment: he did not cause the murders, but he ensured that the guilty did not get away with them (verse 24). Readers also note that the evil was already present in both parties; God's act exposed and turned it back on them.

questions: Jotham's fable says the good trees were too busy bearing fruit to rule. What does that suggest about power and the people who seek it?
Abimelech appealed to family loyalty to gain power. How can loyalty to our own group lead us into wrongdoing?
The chapter shows evil returning on those who commit it. Where have you seen that principle at work, and where does it seem not to hold?
